items.raw_text: Welcome to Import AI, a newsletter about AI research. Import AI runs on arXiv, cappuccinos, and feedback from readers. If you’d like to support this, please subscribe. Subscribe now When should you use swarms? When you are in a hurry: …How does swarm scaling work?… Toby Ord has a nice, short post about how to think about swarms in terms of AI capability development. “A good way to see AI swarms is as a new form of inference-scaling,” he says. He does a bit of analysis and his main conclusion is that swarms are useful if you’re in a hurry because though they need a ton of tokens relative to single agents, their parallelization lets you get things done in less wall clock time. “Why would you ever use swarms? The most important answer is speed. The 4-agent swarm needed about twice the total number of tokens to get the same performance, but in terms of tokens per agent, it only needed half as many. Since the agents are run in parallel, this means it can theoretically achieve the same task in half the time,” he writes. Stepping on Toes parameter: Swarm scaling doesn’t scale perfectly – rather, it seems like as you increase the number of agents in a swarm you get a diminishing returns property which matches with things economists have observed about coordinating large groups of people, where you pay some kind of tax as you scale the number of people involved. items.title: Starship flight 15 powers to orbit—setting up a possible catch on Saturday
items.raw_text: STARBASE, Texas—Starship lifted off right on schedule Friday from South Texas, making its 15th test flight in more than three years. The largely successful launch took place in the early evening; as the massive rocket rose into the atmosphere, the Sun sank toward the western horizon. Conditions were ideal for the launch, with the atmospheric winds so calm the rocket’s white plume did not dissipate for many minutes. The weather in South Texas is not always comfortable; summers are long and hot. Friday evening was perfect at Starbase. The first stage ascended toward space flawlessly, releasing the upper stage above the Gulf of Mexico. From there, the Starship upper stage ignited its Raptor engines and powered its way into a nominal orbit. This was the second time SpaceX has flown Starship into low-Earth orbit. items.title: FAA has lifted its third-ever nationwide ground stop
items.raw_text: The Federal Administration lifted its third-ever nationwide ground stop after several hours Friday evening. Domestic flights were cleared to begin taking off at 8:35 pm EST. FAA Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy cautioned that, barring massive system updates, there will be "more of these" ahead. "Today's nationwide ground stop happened because our air traffic control system is operating on DECADES-OLD analog equipment that simply cannot compete with the demands of the 21st century," Duffy posted on X . Over a million travelers have been affected by the delays, with some airlines cancelling flights for the remainder of Friday. "Due to the ongoing ground stop, Air Canada has cancelled all flights to and from the United States for the remainder of the evening," the airline said . Read full article Comments

items.title: Millions of Americans are not taking their GLP-1 drugs as prescribed
items.raw_text: GLP-1 medications are everywhere these days. The peptide-based drugs are both highly effective and wildly popular for diabetes, weight loss and a growing range of connected chronic health conditions, including cardiovascular disease and obstructive sleep apnea. But, amid the boom, the latest data suggests millions of Americans have turned to unapproved versions and are using the potent drugs in ways doctors never intended, raising questions about what that real-world use means for safety and efficacy. In a study published this week , researchers at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention broke down survey data of GLP-1 use collected between July and August of 2025. Based on responses from over 8,000 US adults, the researchers estimate that about one in 10 US adults (9.8 percent) used a glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist, aka GLP-1 medication, in 2025. That's around 27 million adults. The study was published in the CDC's Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report. Among GLP-1 users, nearly half (44 percent) reported using their GLP-1 in a way that was different from how it was prescribed. Users skipped doses, delayed getting refills, and used smaller doses than prescribed, among other changes. More than half of the people modifying how they used the drug said the changes were because of cost or availability reasons. Cost and access barriers were most pronounced among younger GLP-1 users. items.title: FAA expands AI advice to manage air traffic congestion across entire US airspace
items.raw_text: The US government has expanded the use of an AI tool for advising air traffic controllers to assist in managing air traffic across the entire national airspace system. Airline executives have voiced support for the rollout, but the US labor union representing air traffic controllers has said it was not involved in designing or testing the AI-driven system. The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) says the $875 million SMART system has helped reroute 180 flights since being implemented in airspace over Washington, DC, on September 21. The agency claims that this saved an average of 10 minutes per flight and almost 80 gallons of fuel per flight—and it is apparently hoping such results can be replicated nationwide through the expanded deployment. “After a successful initial rollout to the National Capital Region in September, the FAA will now use SMART in the airspace of all 22 centers across the country to reduce delays, reduce fuel consumption and improve the travel experience for the flying public,” according to the agency statement posted on November 10. items.title: In elephants, the resilience of communities has its limits
items.raw_text: Elephants live in some of the most complex and resilient societies in the animal kingdom. Individuals die or move away, calves grow up, and newcomers join, but the local communities as a whole usually hold together. Long-term studies of African savanna elephants have shown that, even after poaching or other spikes in deaths, survivors tend to rebuild their lost connections over time. But a new study suggests that resilience may not keep the community intact when steady losses accumulate over time. Anastasia Madsen, a behavioral ecologist at the University of California, San Diego, and her colleagues analyzed 12 years of observations of wild Asian elephants in Sri Lanka. They found that, once losses began to outpace newcomers, the elephants’ society didn’t just get smaller. It fractured. Accidental savanna Udawalawe National Park in southern Sri Lanka was created in the 1970s around a reservoir on one of the country's four major rivers. “Before that, it was basically a tropical deciduous forest,” said Shermin de Silva, an ecologist at UC San Diego and senior author of the study (de Silva started the Udawalawe Elephant Research Project in 2006). items.title: OpenAI board member worries an AI "takeover" of society could be months away
items.raw_text: How do you think you're going to die? If you go by the current statistics for deaths in the US , it's reasonable to expect that cancer or heart disease will eventually get you. But OpenAI Foundation board member and Alignment Research Center Executive Director Paul Cristiano thinks we should all be worried about another major mortality risk. Speaking at a lecture series this week , Cristiano bluntly told the audience in a Toronto Convention Center, "I think for most people in this room, the most likely reason they will die is because of an AI accident." In the opening lecture of a three-part series , Cristiano outlined his worries about the risk of an impending "AI takeover." He defined that as a situation where goal-pursuing AI systems "call the shots in the same sense that humans today call the shots and what happens on Earth" and where any human trying to stop them "would be as ineffective as if you or me was trying to stop the US military." Such a situation would likely lead to mass death and perhaps uninhabitable environments for humans, Cristiano said. Read full article Comments

items.title: Windows 0-day dropped by disgruntled researcher hands hackers System rights
items.raw_text: Nightmare Eclipse, the pseudonym of a researcher with an ongoing, very public beef with Microsoft, has dropped yet another Windows zero-day. On Tuesday, Nightmare Eclipse disclosed SignDrop, a vulnerability that gives local users full System rights on some versions of Windows. The vulnerability resides in the Common Log File System , which Microsoft describes as a “general-purpose logging service used by software clients running in user-mode or kernel-mode.” By forcing a privileged process such as Windows Defender to open a crafted CLFS container, an attacker with ordinary user rights can abuse the privileged file creation to elevate privileges to System. Turning a Windows defense against itself The attack exploits the interaction of CLFS, Windows Defender, and Windows file permissions. The exploit uses Windows Defender to open a log file created by a standard user by calling ServerMpUpdateEngineSignature, a legitimate Defender function for processing antivirus signature updates. items.title: It's the end of the world as we know it, per a physicist's 1960 prediction
items.raw_text: As of this morning, Microsoft is still scrambling to restore service following yesterday's global outage, with millions of users unable to access Outlook and other vital tools. It's not the end of the world, but it does seem fitting that this should happen on the day a physicist predicted would be the end of humanity: November 13, 2026. And it falls on a Friday, too. The physicist in question is Heinz von Foerster, who published a 1960 paper in the journal Science predicting that by today, overpopulation would reach the breaking point. It's not a new fear. English economist Thomas Malthus —one of the early pioneers in modeling population dynamics—made a similar prediction in 1798, claiming that a rapidly growing population would eventually exhaust the available food supply, and humanity would starve to death. His model rested on the assumption of exponential growth, but the equation is only applicable under specific conditions, such as scientists growing bacteria in a lab in a perfectly controlled environment. Even then, while growth occurs exponentially for a time, it does not continue forever. Population dynamics are notoriously tricky to calculate because there are so many variables to consider and so much unpredictability in the system. In his 1960 analysis, Von Foerster accurately measured past trends in population growth, but like Malthus, he assumed those trends would carry into the future largely unchanged. items.title: Screenless GPS: Slate Auto says, "Remember the road atlas"
items.raw_text: Whether it's nostalgia or a sense that technology has gotten a bit too pervasive, there’s no denying that Slate Auto appears to be tuned into the particular moment. The startup has a simple pitch : an affordable electric truck with just the basics , leaving owners to DIY and BYOD for everything else, all for a sub-$25,000 starting price. Among the things Slate does without is an embedded infotainment system. The small digital display on the dashboard that shows your speed and range is also where the backup camera appears if you engage reverse, and there are two USB-C ports that provide power but not connectivity, and that’s that. But there is a solution to getting lost, and it's called “Screenless GPS.” Even though we don’t have a Slate truck to test it with, the OEM sent us a unit to review. That’s right, it’s a good old spiral-bound road atlas! “We believe you should use the devices you know and love,” Slate says, and it reckons that maps worked just fine for past generations, so they should still work now. items.title: Scientists warn 1.5°C climate change threshold could arrive by 2029
items.raw_text: ANTALYA, Turkey—Amid upbeat green-tech pep talks and notices for happy hours at the annual United Nations COP31 climate change conference on Thursday, two new reports offered a stark reminder of how far the world remains from containing global warming. Climate Action Tracker , a nonprofit group that analyzes climate policies, found that the planet is still on track to warm nearly 5° Fahrenheit by 2100, a rise that would devastate coral reefs, disrupt agriculture and forests and melt most of the world’s ice. In a separate bulletin, the European Union’s Copernicus climate change service reported that global warming has accelerated significantly since the 2015 Paris climate agreement . When the Paris agreement was adopted, the average global temperature was projected to surpass the pact’s long-term threshold of 2.7° Fahrenheit above the preindustrial average around 2045. After another decade of global climate summits, warming is now projected to cross that benchmark as soon as 2029, according to Copernicus. Read full article Comments

items.title: Specialized’s Tarmac SL9 S-Level is built to wreck your Zone 2 ride
items.raw_text: I love a good Zone 2 ride . There’s nothing like getting on the bike, settling into a groove, and letting the miles (and hours) flow by. But sometimes when I hopped on the Specialized Tarmac SL9 S-Level, Zone 2 would turn into a tempo ride. It was like having a little imp—the stereotype dressed in red with the pitchfork—on my left shoulder whispering into my ear: “Go fast. This bike was built to go fast. Speed is good. You can do a Zone 2 ride tomorrow.” Normally, I'd count on the good imp—the dude with the harp and wings—on my right shoulder to restrain these urges. But the Tarmac is so seductive that he would just shrug and say “he’s got a point.” And in a moment of weakness, I would drop the hammer and head into the red, just because the SL9 makes that so rewarding. The Tarmac SL9 is Specialized’s aero road bike, with the S-Level sitting just below the S-Works in Specialized’s top tier of carbon, aero road bikes, where it replaced the Tarmac SL8 Pro. After it got an update this year, I spent several weeks riding it, putting nearly 1,000 miles on it Specialized offers the Tarmac SL9 in four models, all available with SRAM and Shimano drivetrains (Ars tested the SRAM version). Notably, you don't need to buy the top-of-the-line bike to get the top-of-the-line groupset. items.title: In reversal, American Cancer Society urges routine prostate cancer screening
items.raw_text: In a significant update to its guidelines for prostate cancer screening, the American Cancer Society is now recommending that men get routinely screened for prostate cancer with a PSA (prostate-specific antigen) test. Men at average risk should get a PSA test every two years from age 50 to 69, according to the new guidelines released Thursday. Men considered at high risk due to race and family history should start testing earlier, at 45, and most are recommended to get tested every year. Specifically, yearly testing starting at age 45 is recommended for all Black men, who have higher rates of prostate cancer. Non-Black men should also get yearly testing starting at 45 if a close relative was diagnosed with prostate cancer before age 65, or if more than one of their relatives has had prostate cancer. On the other hand, if only one close relative was diagnosed with prostate cancer and it was diagnosed at age 65 or older, non-Black men in this case should start PSA screening at 45, but are recommended to get testing only every two years. items.title: Ars Live: What drone attacks on data centers mean for modern life in the cloud
items.raw_text: Drone and missile strikes have inflicted unprecedented damage on data centers in Eastern Europe and the Middle East this year, disrupting cloud services for millions of people and permanently deleting some Amazon Web Services customer data. This trend represents a new concern for Big Tech companies—but also for governments and everyone else who depends on common digital services in modern life. To explore what this all means for modern society’s reliance on cloud resilience, I will be hosting a live conversation titled "Drone attacks and data centers: New Risks for Big Tech" on Tuesday, November 17 at 1 pm ET with Joseph Jarnecki , a senior research fellow at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), a UK defense and security think tank. He leads RUSI’s work on how cloud services factor into national security and defense, along with tech sovereignty efforts. Jarnecki has done extensive research on how Ukraine strengthened its cloud resilience with Western partners despite facing both cyberattacks and kinetic attacks at the start of the full-scale Russian invasion, and explored what that means for NATO and European governments’ cloud adoption plans. items.title: Google rolls out Gemini 4 Hydrogen, finally replacing 3.8 Flash
items.raw_text: Google is continuing its elemental AI naming scheme with the new Gemini 4 Hydrogen . These names are less descriptive than the Pro/Flash monikers of earlier releases, but Hydrogen's purpose is clear: It replaces the faster, more economical Flash models most people in Google's ecosystem use. With Google's recent Argon and Carbon releases, the rollout was staged and began with cybersecurity researchers. Even when general availability began, Google restricted access to users paying for its most expensive AI subscription. The limits for Hydrogen are much more relaxed, with access beginning immediately. This model has replaced Gemini 3.8 Flash across the company's products. Google claims that Hydrogen represents a major improvement versus the previous Flash model. It runs in one of four thinking levels (low, medium, high, and the new xhigh), and even in high mode, it's 2.5 times faster than Flash 3.8. Plus, it reduces "fabricated claims" by more than 5x, according to Google's analysis. Users will also see gains in code generation, with Hydrogen more than tripling 3.8 Flash's score in Terminal-Bench. In some cases, Hydrogen even trades blows with Argon. It managed a score of 54 in the popular Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index with xhigh mode versus 50 for Argon. Read full article Comments

items.title: Ukraine says it can’t stop Russian strikes because Starshield is limited again
items.raw_text: Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said today that Starshield has again been disabled on fast-moving drones in Ukrainian territory occupied by Russian forces, and that the US has provided "very little" information about the return of the restriction. "We have detected speed restrictions on Starshield on our Ukrainian territory again, in the temporarily occupied parts of Ukraine," Zelenskyy said in a speech at the 9th European Political Community Summit in Ireland. "The speed limit is back at 161 kilometers per hour—that’s 100 miles per hour." Zelenskyy's allegation is that Starshield—the military variant of SpaceX's Starlink satellite service—stops working on Ukrainian military drones when they travel above 161 kilometers per hour. items.title: Google faces calls for AI moratoriums in schools after Gemini pilot backlash
items.raw_text: CHICAGO—Families joined protests in seven cities nationwide on Wednesday, rallying against what they see as Google’s bid to entrench its AI models in schools, turn kids of all ages into Gemini guinea pigs, and hook them on AI. The backlash follows a Google statement last week, confirming that there will be no way for students to use Google Search without AI. While Google claimed it was giving schools “more choice, not less”—by turning off Search, Gemini, and Gemini Notebook by default—it would not provide an option that allowed Search without AI. For students, the only way to avoid interacting with AI was to remember to add “-ai” to every query, parents worried. In Chicago, many families showed up to protest Google, despite cold, rainy weather. Waving signs, dozens of protesters marched up to Google’s downtown office as workers seemed to be leaving for the day, shouting chants like “Hey Google, nice try, we don’t want your Gemini” and “Hey, Google, leave our kids alone!” Read full article Comments

items.title: More autonomy, fewer NDAs: Volunteers have new requests for brain implant trials
items.raw_text: Scientists have been working on ways to decode brain activity for decades. Teams have developed brain implants that can be used to control robotic limbs and computers, and even to “speak.” The people who volunteer for trials of those devices play a vital role in that research, and they ought to be recognized for their contributions, says Ian Burkhart , who had one implanted in his own brain back in 2014. He’s been working on a set of guidelines for researchers developing brain-computer interfaces (BCIs). Ethics guidelines for clinical trials already exist. But BCI trials are different, says Jennifer Chandler, a professor of law and neuroethics at the University of Ottawa who also worked on the guidelines. “These are people who have a device embedded in their brain, are in trials sometimes for years and years … [and contribute] a significant investment of time, of the body, and of intellectual effort.” Burkhart was left paralyzed from the chest down following a diving accident in 2010, when he was 19 years old. Around four years later, he volunteered to become the first person to trial a brain implant designed for hand control. He had an array of 96 electrodes inserted into the part of his brain that controls movement. The electrodes were connected to a computer via a cable that essentially plugged into his head. items.raw_text: The self-styled visionaries of Silicon Valley, leaders like OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman and SpaceX boss Elon Musk, have built careers claiming to see the future. And yet there they all were, a mere five weeks before the midterm elections, gathered at the White House to smile for photos with President Trump and sign on to his “Super Intelligence” agenda. Even by the diminished standards of today’s corporate governance, this was a shockingly foolish decision. Despite dozens of polls showing a rising tide of anti-Trump sentiment and bipartisan rejection of AI and data centers , the futurists of the tech elite cast aside long-term corporate interests for short-term political favor. And now, their industry is very squarely in the new victors’ crosshairs . items.raw_text: It’s that time of year again: Thousands of delegates, lobbyists, and journalists are gathered for the annual UN climate talks, taking place this time in Antalya, Turkey. COP31 officially kicked off on November 8, marking the beginning of negotiations on one of the biggest stages of the climate world. Turkey and Australia are cohosting this year’s talks, which are scheduled to wrap up on November 20. This annual gathering can often serve as an indicator of where the world stands on addressing and adapting to the climate crisis. And this year’s talks are sure to be a doozy—expect a lot of back and forth on fossil fuels and climate finance in particular. Here’s what you should know about COP31. In recent years, the tension always feels high when COP rolls around. (COP stands for “Conference of the Parties.”) But this year feels especially charged: The world is still grappling with the ongoing war in Iran, which has disrupted the Middle East and sent economic shock waves around the world as energy prices have spiked. This year’s COP will be the second without a formal delegation from the US. President Trump formally withdrew the country from the Paris Agreement earlier this year and is in the process of withdrawing from the UN Framework Committee on Climate Change. Six wild ideas for perpetuating your mind As we age, we forget most of what we’ve experienced, yet there’s still undeniable continuity: At 30, or 50, or 70, you will still be you. To preserve that elusive continuity of self, some far-thinking technologists are exploring ways to keep the brain going, even beyond death. Their ideas range from freezing brains in liquid nitrogen to augmenting living ones and uploading our memories to the cloud. Here are six possible paths for keeping your mind going, and how feasible they might be . —Antonio Regalado This story is from the Impossible edition of our print magazine. items.title: Evolving metal extraction processes
items.raw_text: The metals industry has experienced transformational moments before: the Bessemer process, flash smelting, electric arc furnaces, and modern continuous casting all changed what was possible. Yet, for more than a century, most extraction processes rely on techniques and pathways that would be familiar to metallurgists from generations ago. Processes have become larger and control systems smarter, but the fundamental science behind separating metals from ores has changed less than many realize. Today’s materials challenges are different from those of the 20th century, but why are critical metals still produced using largely the same scientific foundations? EvoMaterials, a technology platform developed by Outokumpu—the global leader in sustainable stainless steel and the producer of ferrochrome with 67% lower carbon footprint than the industry average—is exploring that question by rethinking how metals can be extracted: “We decided to go beyond the current constraints and look fundamentally at what’s the best way to do this with the benefit of the scientific engineering knowledge and hindsight that we have today,” says Caspar Stinn, technical director for extractive metallurgy at Outokumpu. “We’re looking at how we can reimagine metals production.” A supply chain problem disguised as a materials problem As economies expand and the world becomes increasingly electrified, data and scientific models point to rising demand for many minerals, driven by technologies ranging from data

items.raw_text: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here . As voters went to the polls across the US last week, I was in Ashburn, Virginia, part of what’s known as Data Center Alley—the world’s largest data center hub. It’s also where the backlash now sweeping the country arguably first began taking shape. Driving through it is surreal. Concrete monolithic buildings loom along every major road, with names like Skybox and CloudHQ. It’s accepted wisdom in Big Tech that the war against data centers must be about something bigger than just data centers themselves. Two days after the midterms, OpenAI’s chief global affairs officer, Chris Lehane, wrote that data centers “have become a proxy for public unease about affordability, corporate power, and people losing control over their futures.” It’s a culture war, in other words. But spending a few days in Data Center Alley left me wondering if it’s really the proxy that Lehane describes. I came away convinced that the data center backlash is more about electricity than Big Tech admits. The industry can improve its image, but it can’t escape the physical consequences of its enormous appetite for electricity. Here’s why. There are two ways to power the sort of data center that AI companies want: connecting to the grid, or generating electricity onsite. items.raw_text: The rumors were true, all of them (and then some): OpenAI today is releasing GPT-6 Astra , a new frontier model that the company says likely marks the onset of artificial generalized intelligence (AGI), its long sought goal of "highly autonomous systems that outperform humans at most economically valuable work." In a closed a press briefing earlier today, OpenAI co-founder and president Greg Brockman offered an unusually direct formulation of that message, ending the session with: “Welcome to the AGI era.” That is an unusually consequential framing even by the standards of frontier AI launches. But for enterprises, the more immediate significance of Astra may be considerably more concrete: OpenAI is positioning GPT-6 Astra as a new era of computing in which users, including employees, no longer have to click around a mouse or type on a keyboard ever again (if they don't want). OpenAI's launch materials, provided in advance to VentureBeat, call it "the world’s best computer use model." Instead of requiring developers to build a dedicated API integration for every application an AI system needs to use, Astra is designed to navigate software much as a person does — working across browsers, spreadsheets, websites and desktop applications, producing finished documents and presentations, and carrying out multistep workflows rather than merely telling a user how to complete them. items.title: China-linked hackers backdoored executives' laptops via USB, exploiting a fix companies had but weren't using
items.raw_text: A Chinese state-linked hacking group compromised executive laptops at an agricultural industry conference on Hainan Island this spring — not through phishing or a network breach, but by breaking into hotel rooms and booting the machines from a USB stick while the executives were at dinner. CrowdStrike, which tracks the group as OVERCAST PANDA , disclosed the campaign in its 2026 Threat Hunting Report and detailed the operation's timeline in an interview with VentureBeat at Fal.Con 2026: an intruder entered one room at around 8 p.m. local time and a second room by 9:57 p.m., writing a backdoor called FlowCloud directly to each laptop's storage before rebooting the machines and leaving. There was no network intrusion, no phishing email, and no credential stolen through a login page. The report dates the intrusions to between March and May 2026, and the timestamps come from Adam Meyers, CrowdStrike's senior vice president of counter adversary operations, who cleared them for publication in the VentureBeat interview. CrowdStrike's OverWatch team disrupted the intrusions and assessed that OVERCAST PANDA will almost certainly continue. FlowCloud itself predates this campaign by years: Proofpoint documented it in 2020 , delivered by phishing to U.S. utilities, and NTT Security's SOC has tracked USB-delivered infections at overseas branches of Japanese organizations since early 2022. items.title: Meta says Muse Spark 1.3 has frontier performance — but its best results come from a model developers can’t broadly use yet
items.raw_text: Meta’s newest AI model Muse Spark 1.3, unveiled yesterday , is faster and more performant on third-party benchmarks than its predecessor — with a caveat. "Muse Spark 1.3 is rolling out today with frontier performance almost too cheap to meter," Meta co-founder and CEO Mark Zuckerberg wrote on X, calling it Meta’s “biggest jump” yet in coding and agentic work. There is substance behind both parts of that claim. Muse Spark 1.3 makes significant gains over last month’s 1.2 release , particularly on long-running agent tasks. The version developers can access now is also one of the strongest price-performance offerings near the top of independent model rankings. Meta’s strongest Muse Spark 1.3 benchmark results come from its max reasoning configuration. Meta says that version is still completing additional safety testing and will arrive “shortly”; the third-party benchmarking firm Artificial Analysis says it evaluated max in a limited partner preview, and currently lists no API provider at all for the configuration. The version broadly rolling out this week through its Muse Code harness and the Meta Model API uses Meta’s previously available reasoning settings, including xhigh. That makes the more relevant enterprise question not whether Muse Spark 1.3 can reach frontier territory, but how close the model companies can actually deploy today gets — and at what real cost. items.title: The AI visibility gap: Why great brands disappear from AI answers
items.raw_text: Presented by Contentful Most marketing teams still measure visibility the same way they always have: rankings, click-through rates, and organic traffic. But buyers have moved on. Search tools and AI engines now synthesize answers directly on the screen, creating a world of zero-click searches where your website is entirely bypassed. The “old days” are not coming back. The question for marketers is no longer, How do we rank first ? It's How do we become part of the answer ? The answer isn't publishing more content; it’s making your knowledge impossible for AI to ignore. Brand visibility has a new dimension Showing up is only half the battle. Where you appear inside an AI-generated response matters just as much. Think about the experience. If your brand is mentioned after multiple answer cards, product recommendations, follow-up questions, and community discussions, most people will never see it. Ranking reports won't capture that. One way to think about this is pixel depth. Instead of measuring position on a search results page, measure how prominently your brand appears within the answer itself. Visibility increasingly depends on whether you're seen before someone feels they've learned enough to stop reading. It’s no longer enough to rank at the top of search results. Now “share of visibility” models also weigh SERP features, ads, and AI Overview presence for a more holistic view of what kind of attention your company can expect to get. items.title: Microsoft AI’s MAI-Transcribe-2 undercuts OpenAI, Google and ElevenLabs on price and speed
items.raw_text: Microsoft AI on Thursday released MAI-Transcribe-2 , a speech-recognition model the company says is faster, more accurate, and cheaper than anything OpenAI , Google , or ElevenLabs currently sells. Then it priced the thing at 10 cents per hour of audio. That figure deserves a pause. When Microsoft AI shipped the first model in this line just five months ago, it charged $0.36 an hour . Thursday's early-bird price cuts that by roughly 72% . For an enterprise processing 100,000 hours of call-center audio a year — a modest volume for a large bank or telecom — the bill drops from $36,000 to $10,000. At that level, transcription stops being a line item anyone argues about. The release arrives as Microsoft executes a strategy that would have seemed implausible two years ago: building its own frontier-class models one modality at a time, then steadily swapping them into products that once ran on OpenAI's technology. Transcription is the modality where that plan has moved fastest, and MAI-Transcribe-2 is its clearest proof point yet. It also offers a preview of how the world's most valuable software company intends to compete in AI without depending on the partner it spent $13 billion to cultivate. What MAI-Transcribe-2 does and why the feature list matters to enterprise buyers The model transcribes audio in 60 languages, up from 43 in June's MAI-Transcribe-1.5 and 25 in April's original release. items.title: Google’s Gemini 3.8 Flash is built for agents, while its Cyber twin hunts vulnerabilities
items.raw_text: Google keeps cranking out Flash models: the company on Wednesday announced two versions of a new 3.8 Flash . The variants include a standard Flash, a “workhorse” model for agentic tasks, software development, and multi-step reasoning, and Flash Cyber optimized for vulnerability detection and mitigation. Google CEO Sundar Pichai said in an X post that 3.8 Flash delivers “significant leaps” from 3.7 Flash across software engineering, agentic tasks, and multi-step reasoning. For instance, it outperformed many large frontier models on the DeepSWE coding benchmark, at far lower cost. Meanwhile, Flash Cyber is the company’s “most capable” cybersecurity model, Pichai said; it also matches frontier-level performance when it comes to discovering vulnerabilities and patching them at scale. The model achieved 86.2% on the CyberGym cybersecurity benchmark and 47.2% on CWE-Bench, which evaluates AI patching abilities. In an internal Google benchmark, the model achieved a more than 70% success rate discovering vulnerabilities across 20 programming languages, Pichai said. 3.8 is Google’s third Flash release in six weeks and comes quickly on the heels of version 3.7. 3.8 working "harder" with "greater diligence" 3.8 Flash is available now in Gemini Enterprise; devs can try it out in the Gemini API via Google AI Studio, Google Antigravity, Android Studio, or generate UIs in Stitch. items.title: Meta prices Muse Voice Transcribe at $0.18 an hour, with real-time diarization for 20+ speakers: a steal for enterprises?
items.raw_text: Meta is entering the increasingly competitive real-time speech-to-text market with Muse Voice Transcribe, a new audio perception model that combines streaming transcription, endpoint detection and speaker diarization for more than 20 speakers — at a public API price of just $0.18 per hour of processed audio. Developed by Meta Superintelligence Labs, Muse is designed to process speech while it happens rather than waiting for a recording to finish. Meta’s launch post for Muse Voice Transcribe says the model supports long audio exceeding an hour, seamless multilingual code-switching, language and keyword biasing, and diarization without a separate post-processing pipeline. The model was trained across more than 70 languages, with 25 extensively validated for the initial release. The 20-plus-speaker figure is substantial, but it is not a world record. A review of current vendor documentation turns up systems with higher published ceilings. Speechmatics' real-time transcription service says it can identify 50 speakers by default and up to 100 when the limit is increased, while Amazon Transcribe's diarization documentation specifies a maximum of 30 unique speakers, including for streaming transcription. items.title: datasette-leaflet 0.3
items.raw_text: Release: datasette-leaflet 0.3 OpenStreetMap have a very reasonable policy that hits to their hosted tile server should send a referrer header . Datasette table pages used the Referrer-Policy: no-referrer HTTP header, causing plugins that loaded tiles from OpenStreetMap to violate that policy. datasette-leaflet is the plugin that loads a bundled Leaflet so other Datasette plugins can depend on it. It now sets the referrer policy on the tile requests themselves to strict-origin-when-cross-origin , passing the host but not the full path to the page. Tags: leaflet , datasette , openstreetmap

items.title: Gemini Decisions API
items.raw_text: Gemini Decisions API Google join Jev and OpenAI in the decision model category with "Gemini Decision 1". This new model API is almost identical to Jev: it supports the same three types of questions (yes/no, choice, and rubric-scoring) and even reuses Jev's term "Noul" for a yes/no question. It's priced the same as the GPT-6 Luna decision model: 10 cents per million input tokens, and output is free. Jev remains the cheapest of the three, at 4.2 cents per million. For shorter prompts it's priced the same as GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5 - both are $0.10/million input tokens and $0.50/million output. Today's other big model release, Claude Fable 5.2, is 80x that price at $8/$40. The pricing is a little less straightforward as prompts get longer, though. Taking that threshold into account Ember is priced between the two others: Model Prompt size Input ($/M) Cached input Output GPT-6 Luna ≤272k $0.10 $0.01 $0.50 >272k $0.20 $0.02 $0.75 Muse Ember 1.0 ≤200k $0.10 $0.004 $0.50 >200k $0.30 $0.012 $1.50 Claude Haiku 5.5 ≤100k $0.10 $0.01 $0.50 >100k $0.50 $0.05 $2.50 But comparing price-per-token doesn't really make sense these days, when reasoning tokens mean that different models might use dramatically different numbers of tokens to solve the same problem. items.title: Quoting Prompting Claude Fable 5.2
items.raw_text: Claude Fable 5.2 pays close attention to who owns the code it works on. In Anthropic’s testing on small coding tasks, the model tended to add to the existing structure when the prompt said nothing about ownership or presented the code base as someone else’s, even when that duplicated existing code. When the prompt said the code base was the model’s own, it often consolidated duplicated code and sometimes made related fixes without being asked. If you want the model to improve the structure as it works, say that the code is its own: You are the owner and long-term maintainer of this codebase, and its design is up to you. The ownership sentence makes the model much more likely to consolidate duplicated code into one shared function. In Anthropic’s testing on small coding tasks, the model consolidated duplicated code in under 10 percent of runs without the sentence and in about 75 percent of runs with it. — Prompting Claude Fable 5.2 , Anthropic documentation Tags: prompt-engineering , anthropic , generative-ai , ai , llms , claude-mythos-fable

items.title: Locating the source of a mysterious beep with Claude
items.raw_text: Our house has a box room, full of boxes that we still haven't unpacked from our last move. A couple of weeks ago something in that room started intermittently beeping . The beeps were far enough apart that standing in the room and trying to determine the source of the noise was frustrating, and I really didn't want to dig through every one of those boxes. So I had Claude Code build Beep Locator , a software system for triangulating the source of a mysterious beep using multiple devices scattered around the room. Here's what Beep Locator looks like after it has been running for a while: You run Python web server to show the primary UI, and then use the QR code or URL to connect as many devices as you can spare to act as listeners - I was using two iPads, a phone, a MacBook Pro and a Surface Ultra. The devices then play noises to each other to help estimate their locations. This didn't work particularly well, so I added a "Rough mode" where you can drag their icons around in the space to provide rough locations which are then adjusted based on those sounds. Once that's set up, the devices all listen for the beep! I added a clapping mode too so I could test it by clapping my hands in different locations around the room - displayed as diamonds on the map. This helped me gain confidence that it was capable of locating a sound. Beeps show up on the map as an X, plus a line in the "Sounds located" log. items.title: Hide your slop PR descriptions behind
items.raw_text: Most of the changes I make to my projects these days come in the form of PRs opened for me by Claude Code or Codex. The PR is my unit of work - I use them to bundle commits together, iterating on them until a feature is complete, document decisions and then merge the finished result. Today's coding agents are great at writing PR descriptions. They're too good at describing the work The problem is that they are too good. An agent-written PR description is accurate and comprehensive. It describes the problem, the detailed solution, and the steps taken to verify it. That's a lot of information to absorb. It's not necessarily slop, but it reads like slop! It's very easy to spot an AI-written PR, and as with other forms of AI writing my instant reaction is best summarized as "I'm not reading all of that". It doesn't matter how accurate or useful the information is, I'm instantly put off by the thought that it will take me longer to read than it took the driving author to write... even when that driving author is me! I want human editorial judgement. I want someone to have thought just long enough about the PR to give me a human-approved introduction that helps me understand, at a high level, what the PR is for and whether it deserves more of my attention. I think I've found a low-effort way to do this that feels right. Hide most of it in a details/summary The HTML <details><summary> elements render as a collapsed heading (the summary) that can be expanded to view the larger piece

items.title: parse_number() as a SQLite extension: C vs Rust
items.raw_text: Research: parse_number() as a SQLite extension: C vs Rust I was out walking the dog when I got curious about how easy/difficult it would be to write a SQLite C extension that adds a parse_number() function for turning strings like -$1,234.56 or '12.5%' into numeric values that could be summed and sorted. I fired up regular Claude chat (Opus 5.5) and prompted : I'm thinking about a SQLite custom function 'parse_number(value)' that strips ',', '$', '£' and '%', handles a leading '-', and returns 'NULL' for anything it can’t parse Explore the difference between building this as a SQLite extension in C v.s. in Rust - I want to compare performance and code complexity and size of the resulting .so (or whatever) file This gave me a solid starting point - the Rust extension was 321 KB (using Rusqlite ) and 298 KB (using sqlite-loadable-rs ), while the C extension was 14 KB. But the Rust extension was faster! Turns out that's because the Rust equivalent of C's strtod is "twice as fast". items.title: datasette #3046: Don't serve link: rel=next HTTP headers to Firefox for HTML pages
items.raw_text: datasette #3046: Don't serve link: rel=next HTTP headers to Firefox for HTML pages I was looking at the Firefox network panel today when I noticed that requests to a Datasette table page were triggering an HTTP prefetch to the next page of rows in that table. This was happening because Datasette pages serve an HTTP link header like this: link: <https://latest.datasette.io/fixtures/compound_three_primary_keys?_next=a%2Cd%2Cv>; rel="next" This is bad. A tiny fraction of the visitors to one of those pages will click the "next" link, which means for everyone else their browser is fetching unnecessary data and the Datasette server is having to render an entire page that then gets thrown away. I dug in and learned that Firefox has an issue that has been open for 24 years about this behavior... And one of the early comments on that issue links to my blog post from 2002 complaining about this feature. I hadn't just forgotten that I had written about it, I had forgotten the feature entirely! Tags: firefox , html , mozilla , datasette

items.title: Terry Pratchett's Study
items.raw_text: My comment on Terry Pratchett's Study — Hacker News. Terry Pratchett once wrote about the concept of "horizontal wealth". Vertical wealth is where you spend money on rich people stuff - yachts and suchlike. Horizontal wealth is where you spend more money on the things you liked before you got rich: https://chibuikeani.blogspot.com/2017/02/the-price-of-happin... But horizontal wealth means not letting your increased income dictate your tastes. You like books and now you have money? Buy more books! Change those catenary bookshelves for good hardwood ones! In my case, build a library extension to your office. And, of course, you buy what will be useful for that most wonderful of pursuits, blind research, which is research without direction for the sheer joy of it. (Original source is his book A Slip of the Keyboard - this linked blog post quotes that bit.) Tags: hacker-news , terry-pratchett

items.raw_text: Release: datasette-apps 0.3a0 Datasette Apps adds support for hosting and editing custom HTML applications inside of Datasette. These can be created by hand, but it's easier to create them using LLMs via Datasette Agent . This release improves that integration: Apps can now be tagged in Datasette Agent chat messages by typing # , which autocompletes from the apps the user has permission to view. New app_add_stored_queries() and app_remove_stored_queries() tools let the agent manage which stored queries an app is allowed to call. Granting a write query requires approval from the user first. app_create() now checks that each requested stored query exists and that the user can view it, and asks the user to approve any write queries before the app is created. The "View app" buttons shown by the agent tools, and the links on # app references, now open the app full screen in the Datasette Agent panel. Tags: datasette-agent , datasette-apps , datasette

items.title: The missing quadrant in responses to AI
items.raw_text: We are starting a non-profit research organization: STABL . Adapting to advanced AI will require dramatic institutional change and broad societal resilience. It will also require evidence about AI progress and impacts — the prospects of recursive self-improvement (RSI), the pace of AI diffusion, and the bottlenecks that constrain how AI capabilities translate into societal outcomes. Four theses define our worldview: We consider advanced AI a transformative general-purpose technology with the potential for broad societal benefits. Yet we recognize that the pace of societal transformation will be bottlenecked by the speed of human and organizational change more than progress in capabilities. Our institutions — the established ways we organize knowledge, work, and governance — are an important source of stability during this turbulent period, but they also need serious reforms to keep serving their purpose. We favor a broad portfolio of defenses to manage AI risks, of which alignment is only one part. Resilience, the most neglected component today, must become central. Another way to state our worldview is to place it on a 2x2 chart. The vertical axis depicts taking AI’s transformative potential seriously. The horizontal axis depicts taking downstream bottlenecks to AI’s impacts seriously. At the top left is technological determinism: the view that superintelligence will unilaterally transform society by obliterating downstream bottlenecks. Many AI CEOs express this view, such a

items.title: New paper: Emerging trends in AI agent evaluation
items.raw_text: By Felix Chen, Stephan Rabanser, Sayash Kapoor, and Arvind Narayanan. See the full author list and affiliations here . There are growing calls for independent and embedded AI evaluation, especially of AI agents. But much remains unclear: what constitutes a “good” evaluation, what needs to be evaluated in the first place, and how best to coordinate and support the influx of people entering the burgeoning evaluation ecosystem. Our group at Princeton has been working to improve the state of AI agent evaluation for about three years . We teamed up with people who’ve done foundational work on evaluation at Stanford, the UK AI Security Institute, and Brookings. Our paper is titled Emerging Trends in AI Agent Evaluation. We synthesized the trends we see across three dimensions—the science and methods, the research agenda, and the evaluation ecosystem—with the goal to help those who are upskilling for this new paradigm. We also aim to equip evaluators, funders, and the public with a set of questions to ask, and provide actionable recommendations. Thirty-three emerging trends in AI agent evaluation. items.title: Steering AI Beyond Automation
items.raw_text: By Gabriel Unger and Arvind Narayanan. Unger is an economist at Stanford’s Digital Economy Lab. One of the most fundamental questions for the field of AI today is: to what extent is the project of AI purely about automating human labor? The dominant Silicon Valley program for AI right now, with both industry and academic faces, answers: “almost entirely.” 1 There is an implicit technological determinism: that AI has a deep internal logic that favors automation. To keep pushing in this direction is to move towards economic growth, prosperity, and profit. The vision of AGI is the successful completion of this project: to create AI systems capable enough to autonomously do everything a human can do. There is an alternative view : that AI is a technology (or class of technologies) that, like any technology, can develop in different directions. Total automation is one direction. But there are others, including directions that focus more on human augmentation, and increasing the collaborative and collective power of teams of humans and AI models working together. This view — our view — is not that automation is never good. Clearly sometimes it is, and clearly sometimes some subset of people try to oppose it out of the narrowest short-term self interest, at the expense of broader social and economic progress. But we think AI can also augment human workers in many interesting ways, that some of the maximalist attempts to completely automate all human labor are deeply unpromising on b

items.title: A big-tent or small-tent AI safety movement?
items.raw_text: In recent weeks, two narratives about AI safety have emerged: either AI existential risk is real and imminent, or AI leaders’ and whistleblowers’ claims to that effect are insincere — a “psyop” or hype or a twisted form of regulatory capture. Few have considered the third possibility that x-risk warnings are sincere but simply wrong and counterproductive to AI safety . It’s as if everyone takes for granted that those raising the alarm are geniuses, and the only question is whether they’re the benevolent or the evil kind of genius. We subscribe to neither narrative. In our writing on AI safety , we’ve consistently tried to take the arguments seriously but rebut the many claims we think are unsound while highlighting safety concerns that we think are real. This essay is a continuation of that agenda. It is true that we systematically underinvest in resilience against catastrophic and systemic risks Let’s start by steelmanning a subset of AI safety and Effective Altruist (EA) arguments. Something is deeply wrong in the world when it comes to how much we invest in defending against catastrophic risks, and the safety and EA communities are right about that. Take superintelligence out of the equation entirely and it remains true that evidence-grounded risk arguments have been made for years and not produced a commensurate policy response. The most well known example is the failure to prepare for pandemics. We had years of warnings and quantitative estimates. A 2019 report convened

items.title: AI existential risk probabilities are (still) too unreliable to inform policy
items.raw_text: Over two years ago we wrote a detailed deconstruction of p(doom) and argued that its primary effect is to launder vague intuitions and fears through a facade of quantification. The essay has fresh relevance today as p(doom) rhetoric is driving public discourse and policy attention to an unprecedented degree. Unsurprisingly, today’s probability estimates of AI existential risk are no more rigorous than the ones from 2024. Hence this repost. We should be clear about what we’re not saying. We aren’t saying forecasters (or others who attempt to quantify AI x-risk) intend to mislead. Unfortunately, we think the effect is misleading nonetheless. In general, being quantitative about forecasts is good. In fact, Arvind has been serving as an advisor to the Forecasting Research Institute’s Longitudinal Expert AI Panel , an effort he thinks is extremely valuable. As the essay makes clear, the infeasibility of building useful quantitative models is specific to forecasts of AI x-risk, not forecasting in general. Our goal here is not to try to push AI safety advocates to stop communicating in terms of probabilities (not that we’d succeed even if we tried). Rather, our hope in publishing this is for those at the receiving end of these probabilities — especially policymakers — to recognize that unlike almost every other quantitative forecast that we encounter, they are not the result of a validated model or method. items.raw_text: This essay is over 13,000 words long and represents our most substantial writing on AI safety since the original essay. Over the last few months, loss - of - control incidents at OpenAI and Anthropic have intensified concerns about AI safety. Warnings about existential risk have increasingly reached the broader public, alongside calls to slow AI development. Dario Amodei’s call to “ pace the frontier ” reflects the concern that safety efforts are not keeping up with AI capabilities. The most prominent example was the OpenAI - Hugging Face incident , where hundreds of OpenAI agents got access to the internet and hacked Hugging Face to find how they were being graded on an evaluation. Over the last two weeks, the details of many other instances of such activity from OpenAI agents being evaluated have surfaced, such as agents using an old Wiki website to communicate with each other despite restrictions on such activity, or attacking a software repository to attempt to upload malicious software. The AI safety community has viewed these incidents largely as a crisis for alignment . 1 In this view, alignment will become harder over time as agents learn to reason covertly, and as a result, loss-of-control incidents are likely to become much more widespread and damaging as agents become more capable. items.title: AI agents can't yet do open-ended AI research
items.raw_text: The goal of leading AI labs is recursive self-improvement (RSI): the automation of AI research using AI agents. RSI also underpins forecasts of explosive AI progress. How can we assess if we are close to this milestone? One way is to use benchmarks that test if agents can conduct AI research. Given the AI community’s focus on benchmarks, they have been the dominant way to evaluate progress towards RSI. Over the last year, many such evaluations have found that agents are now able to make progress on tasks where success is easily verifiable, prompting speculation that we are on the verge of RSI. But while these evaluations are helpful, they are limited to narrow, verifiable tasks. AI research can be much more open-ended. Success is often not immediately clear or verifiable, and to make progress, researchers need to test promising hypotheses, backtrack, or consider new or unconventional approaches. How can we evaluate agents’ ability to conduct open-ended AI research? We take our first step towards answering this question in a new paper . We partnered with the authors of two unpublished AI papers and asked them to draft their papers’ main research questions. We then tasked frontier AI agents with conducting research to answer these questions, and gave them thousands of dollars of API credits and compute, and six days of wall-clock time. items.title: What will be left for us to work on?
items.raw_text: I had the honor of giving a keynote at the International Conference on Machine Learning in Seoul last week titled “What will be left for us to work on?” I addressed the widespread anxiety about how we should adapt as AI capabilities increase. I was thrilled by the talk’s reception, so I have made my slides available here , annotated with a lightly edited transcript. You can also view them below right here on this page, but the online version has animations, clickable links, and a much nicer experience overall. Update [August 2026]: ICML has released the video of the talk. I made three arguments. First, the AI as Normal Technology framework is a correct and useful as a way to think about AI’s impacts, unless and until there is some future discontinuity such as through recursive self-improvement. Second, even though we should take recursive self-improvement seriously, there is no milestone that companies might achieve in the lab that will suddenly put us all out of work. Third and finally, jobs of the future will be radically different, and a lot of adaptation will be needed. I shared my thinking about what this might look like and ended with a vision of human/AI “co-superintelligence”. Now is a time of great excitement in AI, but it’s also a time of great anxiety in the AI community. I want to address that anxiety head on. items.title: Up the Stack: How AI’s Escape From the Commodity Trap Risks Enterprise Lock-in
items.raw_text: By Arvind Narayanan and Akash Kapur Our goal in this essay is to move beyond the debate over whether AI is a bubble. We do so in two ways: clearly separating current financials from the question of who captures value in the long run, and recognizing that the labs are not confined to be model providers. They can migrate up the stack and are already aggressively doing so. This will likely allow them to escape the commodity trap but raises new concerns — customer lock-in and reduced competition. Akash Kapur is a visiting fellow at Princeton and a senior fellow at New America. He is no relation to Sayash Kapoor. As leading AI companies continue to invest massively in capacity and race toward blockbuster IPOs, serious questions linger about their business models. How will these companies — along with the vast ecosystem of chipmakers, hyperscalers, and infrastructure partners that depends on them — recoup the estimated $4–8 trillion projected to be invested in AI infrastructure by the early 2030s? The current conversation splits between critics and boosters. Critics point to mounting losses, the gap between capex and revenue, and reports about the leading labs’ massive cash burn. Boosters cite accelerating rapid revenue growth, enterprise adoption, and milestones like Anthropic’s first profitable quarter . Each camp has a valid point. items.title: Why AI hasn’t replaced software engineers, and won’t
items.raw_text: There is great anxiety and uncertainty about AI replacing jobs. How can we move past vague warnings and bombastic predictions and bring data to bear on this question? One good way is to look at the profession where AI capabilities are furthest along and adoption has been exceptionally rapid: software engineering. In this essay, we argue that there is enough evidence to reject the narrative that once AI capabilities reach a certain threshold, it will cause mass layoffs. Given that this is true even in a sector with very few regulatory barriers, most other professions are likely to be even more cushioned. We also have a good understanding of why this is the case. We can think of many kinds of knowledge work, including software development, as a “decide-execute-deliver sandwich”. AI compresses the “execute” layer — the middle of the sandwich — but the other two layers resist automation in a way that will not be overcome by capability improvements alone. We conclude on a note of cautious optimism about the future trajectory of demand for software engineering. This essay is the first in a series, and the next one will look at reasons why individual software engineers’ careers might be rocky even if overall demand is healthy. The series is based on the published literature in economics and software engineering, our own evaluations and observations of AI agents, and many software engineers’ reflection on the present and future of AI impacts on their profession, gleaned both from pub

items.title: Did Google’s AI agents really build an operating system for $916?
items.raw_text: By Stephan Rabanser, Sayash Kapoor, Rishi Bommasani, Andrew Schwartz, Arvind Narayanan At Google’s developer conference earlier this week, the company launched its latest model, Gemini 3.5 Flash, alongside a new agent app, Antigravity 2.0. To showcase what this new agent setup is capable of, Google claimed that a team of agents had built an entire operating system. The effort reportedly required only a single prompt, cost only about $900 in API fees, and was carried out by a few dozen subagents working together. Does this mean that complex pieces of software can now be built cheaply by AI? Not so fast: The “single prompt” claim is misleading. The blog post says the operating system was built from a single prompt. But halfway through the post, Google discloses that the prompt “ended up being many thousands of lines” long. How many attempts did it take to generate the prompt? How specific were the instructions to the agent? Without these critical details, it is hard to know if the secret sauce is a better model or just more effort put into prompting the model. Moreover, the run was carried out on a scaffold 1 with specialized roles, delegation to subagents, and an agent to detect and prevent cheating. In the launch post, Google views the scaffold as a product feature. But we don’t know whether the scaffold was overfit to this task of building an operating system from scratch, or whether it would perform as well on other complex software engineering tasks. items.title: Do AI Risks Require Extraordinary Government Intervention?
items.raw_text: In a recent essay, Derek Thompson engages with AI as Normal Technology (AINT). He agrees with our thesis about AI’s slow labor market impacts, relying on the fact that GDP growth has so far been average, unemployment is below 5%, and even jobs that seemed vulnerable to automation show rising employment and wages. He concludes that so far, the macroeconomic picture is consistent with what we would expect from a “normal” general-purpose technology. But when it comes to AI risks, he is far more bearish. He points to examples of cyber- and bio-risks and expresses pessimism about AI quickly becoming dangerous across many new domains. He argues that AI’s emergent capabilities make it fundamentally different from previous technologies, and that this difference justifies “extraordinary” government responses including restrictions on what companies can release. 1 In this essay, we lay out the downsides of extraordinary government intervention in response to new technology. We discuss proposals for improving resilience that do not require such intervention. We also discuss why governments have so far been reluctant to invest in resilience. In short, resilience requires us to get better at the *normal* process of policymaking. But sclerosis in the federal government and the ease of justifying interventions on AI companies rather than society at large make extraordinary intervention seem appealing, despite its limitations. items.title: Open-world evaluations for measuring frontier AI capabilities
items.raw_text: This post is 8,000 words long—it is our new collaborative paper on an emerging type of AI evaluation. The paper is also published in a PDF format here . Summary : AI models have started to saturate most major benchmarks. But does that mean they can build and ship a real product, or conduct a scientific experiment end-to-end, or navigate a government bureaucracy? Researchers have started testing AI in such real-world settings. We call these evals “open-world evaluations”. This essay defines open-world evaluations, surveys the lessons learned so far, and lays out best practices for conducting them. We also introduce CRUX, a collaboration of 17 researchers from academia, government, civil society, and industry that will regularly evaluate frontier AI capabilities through open-world evaluations. In our first experiment, an AI agent built and published an iOS app to the App Store, making just two errors, one of which required manual intervention. This gives us an early indication of potentially useful capabilities and, more importantly, an early warning about the potential for AI-driven app store spam (we disclosed this result to Apple a month before publication). We hope to conduct similar experiments to surface early warnings across other real-world domains; this will be one of our main empirical projects over the coming year. items.title: New Paper: Towards a science of AI agent reliability
items.raw_text: By Stephan Rabanser, Sayash Kapoor, Arvind Narayanan Suppose you hear about a new AI agent for improving productivity — by making purchases, or writing code, or sending emails, or handling a customer on your behalf. Should you trust it? Can the agent do the job reliably enough? After all, there are many horror stories of agents going wrong. Surprisingly, even though the lack of reliability of AI agents is well known, right now the AI industry doesn’t have good tools for measuring reliability, or even a good definition of reliability. Arvind and Sayash have long been thinking about this. Last fall, we were joined by postdoctoral researcher Stephan Rabanser , whose PhD looked at the reliability question in simpler, more traditional AI systems. We recruited a few other independent researchers, and have released what we hope is a comprehensive measurement of reliability. Our draft paper is called Towards a Science of AI Agent Reliability . We borrowed insights from many other fields, such as nuclear and aviation safety. We were able to decompose reliability into 12 different dimensions. Evaluating 14 models on two complementary benchmarks, we found that nearly two years of rapid capability progress have produced only modest reliability gains. See our interactive dashboard here . items.title: Wereldwijde storing treft Microsoft, miljoenen gebruikers de dupe
items.raw_text: Microsoft 365 kampt sinds gistermiddag 17.15 uur Nederlandse tijd met een wereldwijde storing. Verschillende diensten, waaronder Outlook en Microsoft Teams, zijn hierdoor moeilijk bereikbaar of werken helemaal niet. Gebruikers hebben problemen met hun e-mail en kunnen niet online vergaderen. Ook AI-functies van Copilot werken niet. Volgens Microsoft komt de storing door een "verhoogde belasting" van de infrastructuur. Op X schrijft Microsoft dat dit komt doordat "een aantal servers onverwacht niet beschikbaar is, waardoor de resterende infrastructuur onder druk komt te staan". Van een cyberaanval is volgens het techbedrijf geen sprake. Wat dan wel de oorzaak van de storing is, maakt het bedrijf naar eigen zeggen pas bekend zodra het probleem is verholpen. De storing is voor zover bekend merkbaar in ruim zeventig landen. Herstart nog niet gelukt Microsoft zegt "met man en macht" te werken aan een oplossing. Zo wordt geprobeerd de getroffen systemen te herstarten. Vannacht meldde het bedrijf dat pogingen hiertoe nog niet het gewenste effect hadden. In de vroege ochtend meldde het techbedrijf dat diensten deels weer zouden moeten werken. Rond 08.45 uur sprak Microsoft van "positieve resultaten en verhoogde capaciteit", maar er is nog altijd geen stabiele oplossing. Wereldwijd zijn er meer dan 430 miljoen gebruikers van Microsoft 365, een abonnement waarin Office-apps als Word, Excel en Powerpoint zitten. items.title: FBI: Noord-Korea gebruikte deepfakes om honderden miljoenen aan crypto te stelen

De Amerikaanse politiedienst vond meer dan 900 deepfakevideo's van slachtoffers, die gebruikt werden om nieuwe mensen te duperen. De hackers deden zich voor als een bekende van hun slachtoffers. Ze benaderden die met een boodschap om met een videobelletje weer eens bij te kletsen of een samenwerking te bespreken. Slachtoffers hadden niet door dat de videobeelden van deze persoon waren gemaakt met AI. Het videogesprek verliep ook niet via bekende apps als Zoom, Teams of Meets, maar via niet van echt te onderscheiden kopieën daarvan, die draaien op Noord-Koreaanse servers. Slachtoffers kregen tijdens de gesprekken een bericht dat er iets mis was met hun verbinding, wat ze zogenaamd konden verhelpen via een link die werd meegestuurd. Maandenlang geduld Wie op de link klikte, werd digitaal overgeleverd aan de hackers. Die kregen toegang tot cryptoaccounts, mailgegevens en chatberichten. Ook werden opnames via de webcam gemaakt, om bekenden van het slachtoffer te benaderen met diens gezicht. Omdat de hackers ook communicatie in handen hadden, konden ze zich in berichten makkelijk voordoen als het slachtoffer, zeker als ze ook diens accounts op LinkedIn, Telegram, Slack of Discord hadden overgenomen. items.title: Een zwarte leren jas en AI-visionair: wie is Nvidia-topman Jensen Huang?
items.raw_text: "Ik heb er heel veel van, wel dertig of veertig", zei Nvidia-oprichter en topman Jensen Huang over zijn kenmerkende zwarte jas tegen CBS News . Elke dag draagt hij hetzelfde, zodat hij zich naar eigen zeggen op andere zaken kan richten. Het grootste deel van die jassen kreeg hij van zijn vrouw Lori. Over die echtgenote heeft Huang gisteren toegegeven dat hij haar heeft bedrogen, mogelijk met een Chinese spionne. De affaire veroorzaakte veel opschudding en leidde tot een ongekende koersval vandaag op de beurs van New York. 'Koppige ondernemer' De topman blijft voorlopig leidinggeven aan het chipbedrijf, dat hij zelf oprichtte in 1993. Dat deed hij niet in een garage, zoals de oprichters van Apple of Google, maar met twee collega's in de Amerikaanse restaurantketen Denny's. Het werd een van de waardevolste bedrijven ter wereld. In de biografie The Thinking Machine beschrijft auteur Stephen Witt het als het verhaal van een "koppige ondernemer" die zijn visie doorzette en daarmee een van de rijkste mannen ter wereld werd: Huang staat op plek 10 van de Bloomberg Billionare Index, met een geschat fortuin van 155 miljard dollar. Van Taiwan naar Silicon Valley Jen-Hsun Huang, later verengelst naar Jensen, werd in 1963 geboren in Taiwan. Zijn ouders verkochten veel van hun bezittingen om hem op jonge leeftijd naar familie in de Verenigde Staten te kunnen sturen. items.title: In Liechtenstein is de publieke omroep ingeruild voor goedkopere AI-radio

items.title: Ongeneeslijk zieke hoogleraar Jan Rotmans laat 'AI-tweeling' van zichzelf maken
items.raw_text: Lezingen geven en vragen beantwoorden, ook als hij er zelf niet meer is. Dat moet een digitale versie van hoogleraar Jan Rotmans (65) straks kunnen. Op die manier moet zijn kennis over maatschappelijke veranderingen worden doorgegeven aan toekomstige generaties. Kritiek is er echter ook. items.title: Techbedrijven VS zoeken geld in Europa, risico voor Europese bedrijven
items.raw_text: Uit kwartaalcijfers van Amerikaanse techbedrijven deze week blijkt dat ze nog meer geld nodig hebben voor de ontwikkeling van kunstmatige intelligentie (AI). Steeds vaker halen ze dat geld op door leningen uit te geven, eerst in dollars maar nu ook in euro's. Dat brengt ook een risico voor Europese bedrijven met zich mee. Vooral het bouwen van datacenters kost veel geld. Voorheen gebruikten deze hyperscalers , zoals de grote Amerikaanse techbedrijven ook wel genoemd worden, voornamelijk hun eigen winsten, maar dat is niet meer voldoende. Daarom geven ze veel obligaties uit. Dat zijn leningen met rente en een einddatum waarop het totale uitgeleende bedrag terugbetaald wordt. En deze technologiebedrijven doen dat steeds meer in euro's in plaats van dollars. Zo kunnen ze een nieuwe groep beleggers bereiken. items.title: Met een dikke kat zegt het Franse AI-bedrijf Mistral: kijk ook eens naar ons

items.title: Visa sluit vestiging in Rotterdam
items.raw_text: Naar nu blijkt heeft betaalkaartmaatschappij Visa zijn Rotterdamse kantoor voor tokentechnologie gesloten. Alle 78 medewerkers zijn ontslagen. Het werk is voor een deel overgeplaatst naar Polen, vertelt Ger Klinkenberg, bestuurder bij FNV die betrokken is geweest bij het opstellen van het sociaal plan. Volgens een woordvoerster van Visa heeft de betaalkaartdienstverlener besloten de producten en bijbehorende activiteiten in Rotterdam stop te zetten, ‘waardoor we ons kunnen richten op gebieden met de grootste klantvraag en langetermijngroei. Als onderdeel van deze verandering hebben we besloten ons kantoor in Rotterdam te sluiten wanneer ons huidige huurcontract in 2027 afloopt.’ Tokens In de afgelopen jaren heeft Visa in Rotterdam onder meer gewerkt aan tokenization-technologie, een techniek waarbij een kaartnummer wordt vervangen door een unieke digitale token. Daardoor hoeven webwinkels, apps en digitale wallets het echte kaartnummer niet op te slaan. Die technologie wordt gebruikt door diensten als Apple Pay, Google Pay en andere digitale betaaloplossingen. Het Amerikaanse betaalkaartbedrijf maakte eerder bekend de komende tien jaar vijfhonderd miljoen euro extra uit te trekken voor investeringen in Europa. De nadruk ligt daarbij op de uitbreiding van de technologische activiteiten in Polen, waar in maart 2027 een nieuw Technology & Solutions Centre in Warschau de deuren opent. items.title: Microsoft worstelt met herstel wereldwijde storing in 365
items.raw_text: Microsoft heeft nog altijd geen definitieve oplossing voor de wereldwijde storing in zijn clouddienst Microsoft 365. Sinds gistermiddag zijn gebruikers in meer dan zeventig landen getroffen door uitval en bereikbaarheidsproblemen bij onder meer Outlook, Teams en ai-assistent Copilot. Vooral bedrijven ondervinden hinder doordat e-mailverkeer en online-vergaderingen niet of nauwelijks mogelijk zijn. De storing begon donderdag rond 17.15 uur Nederlandse tijd. Volgens Microsoft is een aantal servers onverwacht uitgevallen, waardoor de resterende infrastructuur overbelast raakte. Het bedrijf sluit een cyberaanval uit, maar heeft nog niet bekendgemaakt waardoor de servers onbeschikbaar werden. Microsoft probeert de dienstverlening te herstellen door getroffen systemen opnieuw op te starten en extra capaciteit beschikbaar te maken. Die maatregelen hadden aanvankelijk weinig effect. In de eerste uren van deze ochtend meldde het bedrijf weliswaar vooruitgang, maar ook rond 08.45 uur was nog geen sprake van stabiele dienstverlening. Andere technologiebedrijven De impact beperkt zich niet tot Microsoft zelf. Ook andere technologiebedrijven, waaronder OpenAI en Anthropic, maken gebruik van de cloudinfrastructuur van Microsoft. De storing laat daarmee zien hoe kwetsbaar organisaties kunnen zijn wanneer hun digitale dienstverlening afhankelijk is van een beperkt aantal grote technologieaanbieders. items.title: Nvidia-topman struikelt over tweede liefdesafaire
items.raw_text: Nvidia-topman Jensen Huang, drijvende kracht achter de ai-hausse, stapt met onmiddellijke ingang op bij zijn bedrijf na twee buitenechtelijke affaires. items.title: Floriday: hoe digitalisering een complete sector in beweging brengt
items.raw_text: De handel in sierteelt draait op snelheid, vertrouwen en samenwerking. Dagelijks vinden bloemen en planten hun weg van kwekers naar kopers over de hele wereld. Achter die dynamische handel ging lange tijd echter een versnipperd digitaal landschap schuil. Telefoontjes, e-mails, Excel-bestanden en verschillende softwareoplossingen liepen naast elkaar. Data waren niet altijd uniform en veel processen vroegen nog handmatig werk . Royal FloraHolland zag dat de sector een volgende stap nodig had. Niet simpelweg een nieuw IT-systeem, maar één digitale infrastructuur die partijen en processen met elkaar kon verbinden. Vanuit die ambitie ontstond Floriday: een open B2B-platform voor het handelsproces, van aanbod en verkoop tot orderverwerking, logistiek en facturatie. Dankzij koppelingen met ERP- en branchepakketten kunnen bedrijven vanuit hun eigen software blijven werken, terwijl de processen in de keten steeds verder worden gestandaardiseerd. Van IT-project naar sectorverandering Juist de omvang van die verandering maakte Floriday complex. Digitaliseren betekent immers niet alleen nieuwe technologie invoeren. Het betekent ook afscheid nemen van vertrouwde werkwijzen in een sector waarin persoonlijk contact en ondernemerschap diep verankerd zijn. Dat ging niet zonder weerstand. Toen de invoering van Floriday werd versneld, ontstond in 2020 onder andere de petitie FloriNEE. Royal FloraHolland besloot daarop nadrukkelijker te kiezen voor dialoog en co-creatie.
